questions.question: Explain why division of duties is described as converting 'trust in individuals into confidence in a system', using the tuck-shop story as your evidence.
questions.expected_answer: With one person controlling money, stock and records, honesty and theft look identical — nothing can be proven either way. Splitting the roles (one takes money, one hands stock, one records, two count together) means any wrongdoing must survive a second independent pair of hands, and the matching records prove the honest workers honest. The system, not personal trust, produces the confidence.

questions.question: Name the five components of internal control and give the plain question each one answers.
questions.expected_answer: Control environment — who sets the example? Risk assessment — what could go wrong here? Control activities — what rules stop it? Information systems and communication — does everyone know what is happening? Monitoring — who checks that the rules still happen in practice?

questions.question: Describe the three-move method for answering an internal-control scenario question, and apply it to: 'The same employee orders stock, receives deliveries, and pays suppliers.'
questions.expected_answer: Move one, name the weakness in control language: no division of duties — one person controls the whole purchasing cycle. Move two, make the risk concrete: goods could be ordered for private use or payments approved for undelivered goods without detection. Move three, recommend a specific control: separate ordering, receiving (checked against the order) and payment authorisation between different people.
